blocks.content: Fig 1, 'Public health supply chain partners and processes'. Four nested circles. The outer blue circle holds forecasting and planning and traceability, with the Ministry of health, regulators, procurers, manufacturers/distributors and logistics providers on or near its rim. The purple circle holds warehouse management, order management and transportation/distribution, with central and regional warehouses on its rim. summary.text: Introduction describing public health supply chain partners, processes and information flows, the challenges of manual and siloed systems, and the meaning of a digital health supply chain (DHSC); it sets out what the handbook covers, its stepwise four-chapter approach, its alignment with the DIIG and the five SMART Guidelines knowledge layers, how it was developed through consultations in Ethiopia, Malawi and Rwanda and a DH&I WG small working group, and its target audiences (Table 1).

blocks.content: Fig 2, 'Information flow across supply chain processes'. Eight rounded boxes: forecasting and planning, sourcing and contract management, order management, traceability, procurement, warehouse management, transportation and dispensing. Two-headed arrows join them, showing that information flows both ways between the processes; warehouse management is the most connected box.

Fig 3, 'Digital health supply chain'. Six purple hexagons surround an icon labelled Individuals: digital ecosystem, end-to-end visibility, data and analytics, transactional systems, advanced digitization and collaborative processes. A dashed ring around them carries eleven partners as dots: Ministry of health, community health, health facilities, regional warehouses, private sector, central warehouse, regulators, logistics providers, procurers and manufacturers/distributors.

Fig 4, 'The stepwise approach used in this handbook'. Four coloured chevrons in a row: 1. Defining a holistic DHSC strategy; 2. Defining the DHSC architecture; 3. Planning for scalable implementation and sustainable operations; 4. Using the DHSC to implement traceability. Chevron 1 lists four steps (identify and engage stakeholders, analyse the current state of HSCISs, define the vision and strategic goals, define a strategic roadmap and performance indicators). Chevron 2 lists three (assess the current state of HSCISs, define a target architecture, identify implementation activities and map them to strategic goals). Chevron 3 lists four (plan the implementation, develop an operational plan, develop a budget, and implement each intervention). The crop also includes the chapter list and a 'Before using this handbook' box above the figure.

Fig 5, 'DIIG process for planning and implementing a digital health enterprise'. Seven numbered, colour-coded phases — from 01 assessing the current state and enabling environment to 07 implementing, maintaining and scaling — each with its steps. To the right, resource tiles are placed against the phases they serve and marked as PDF or online, including the WHO–ITU eHealth strategy toolkit, the Digital implementation investment guide, the ITU SDG digital investment framework, TOGAF, OpenHIE, the WHO SMART guidelines with digital adaptation kits, and the WHO MAPS toolkit. 'WHO handbook for health supply chain architecture (this document)' is highlighted twice: spanning phases 02 to 04, and in phase 07. Adapted from the 2020 WHO Digital Implementation Investment Guide.

Fig 6, 'WHO SMART Guidelines approach'. A top band of five knowledge layers, each fed from a research and evidence base: L1 narrative (enhanced guidelines), L2 operational (digital adaptation kits), L3 machine-readable (machine-readable recommendations), L4 executable (reference software) and L5 dynamic (precision health models). A localisation bar leads down to five matching country adaptations: national policies and procedures, localized requirements, localized machine-readable code and standards, localized digital services, and dynamic applications trained for local outcomes. These feed data, evidence and impact, and an 'Evidence from digital implementations' arrow returns to the research base. Source: adapted from WHO SMART Guidelines.

Fig 7, 'Sample workflow for an antenatal care business, with connections to the supply chain highlighted'. A BPMN diagram with client and health worker lanes: arrival, registration, rapid assessment, danger signs, pregnancy confirmation, quick check, profile and history, the ANC assessment group, the counselling and treatment group (10.1 to 10.9), referral, scheduling and self-care. An enlarged inset shows the tasks outlined in purple as connected to the supply chain: 9 conduct laboratory tests and imaging, 10.5 nutrition supplementation, 10.7 immunizations and 10.9 deworming and malaria counselling and prophylaxis. Source: adapted from the 2021 WHO Digital Adaptation Kit for Antenatal Care.

summary.text: Chapter 1 opening on defining a holistic DHSC strategy, listing guiding principles informed by the Principles for Digital Development (national priority alignment, user-centred approach, interoperability, stakeholder engagement, reuse, scalability and sustainability), the expected outputs (vision, strategic goals, objectives and roadmap), and the need to align the DHSC strategy with national IT, health, medicines, supply chain and digital health strategies.

blocks.content: Fig 8, 'Alignment of national strategies'. Nested arrow shapes, each ending in VISION. The health strategy contains the health supply chain strategy, which contains the medicines and health product strategy. The digital/IT strategy contains the digital health strategy. The digital health supply chain strategy sits where the two families overlap.

blocks.title: Why is a strategy necessary?
blocks.content:
A holistic DHSC strategy is essential to achieving 
comprehensive digital transformation of the health supply 
chain. It can offer a clear vision and direction and ensure 
alignment across all national digital transformation 
initiatives (Fig. 8) (21). Such initiatives may include the 
following:
	
→national health strategy, which establishes a vision 
and priorities to address the most pressing health 
care challenges and improve health care for the 
population; 
	
→national medicines and health product policies, which 
aim to increase access to and use of high-quality, 
affordable medicines

summary.text: Chapter 1 section on why a DHSC strategy is necessary, describing the national strategies it should align with (Fig. 8), the risks of forgoing a guiding vision and strategy, such as fragmented and noninteroperable systems, inconsistent product nomenclature (Fig. 9), nonscalable systems and duplicative implementations, and introducing the four steps for developing the strategy.

blocks.content: Fig 9, 'Inconsistent use of standardized product nomenclature across the supply chain'. A dashed arrow marks the physical flow of health products from manufacturers through the central warehouse, health facilities and community health workers to patients. Below, each holds the same product under a different code: product code 123123 at the manufacturer, A1232 in mSupply, P44545 in eLMIS and AM545 on paper forms, joined by broken chain-link icons.

blocks.title: Is a DHSC architecture necessary?
blocks.content:
The health supply chain comprises several business 
processes that ensure the availability of health products 
to individuals. Forecasting and supply planning processes 
ensure adequate supply to meet demand. Procurement and 
distribution processes ensure that medicines and health 
products are sourced and delivered to the right locations 
and are available to individuals when needed. Warehouse 
management processes support receiving, storage and 
management of inventory. 
Health supply chains should be able to quickly respond to 
exceptions such as stockouts and quality issues like product 
r

summary.text: Chapter 2 section on whether a DHSC architecture is necessary, describing the health supply chain business processes it must support, the national- and subnational-level capabilities the architecture defines, and how it enables end-to-end visibility of the supply chain and the ability to track, trace and verify health products.

blocks.title: What are the risks of forgoing a DHSC architecture?
blocks.content:
The lack of an overarching DHSC architecture leads to risks 
such as those listed below:
	
→siloed and duplicative systems that lack the ability to 
adapt and scale, requiring more effort and money to 
maintain and sustain;
	
→lack of compliance with global and open standards, 
resulting in a lack of interoperability among processes, 
systems and data, which in turn, affects the timely 
availability of aggregated data for visibility, analysis, 
exception management, reporting and decision-
making;
	
→laborious manual processes for aggregating, 
reconciling and triangulating data for accurate

summary.text: Chapter 2 section on the risks of forgoing a DHSC architecture, including siloed and duplicative systems, noncompliance with global and open standards, laborious manual data aggregation and limited traceability, followed by the three steps for defining the architecture and a figure on end-to-end visibility and track and trace across global and national levels (Fig. 11).

blocks.content: Fig 11, 'Health supply chain end-to-end visibility and traceability'. Product flows from manufacturing and shipping through customs, central warehouse receiving and inventory management, distribution, regional warehouse replenishment and health facility dispensing to individuals, with forecasting and planning, supplier and contract management, procurement and order management above. Arcs mark end-to-end visibility at country and global level, and arrows below mark track and trace at national and global level.

summary.text: Chapter 2 Step 2 covering definition of a target DHSC architecture, with inputs, tasks, outputs and mitigations, a best practice on capturing actual consumption at the last mile, the DIIG enterprise architecture (Fig. 13) and the DHSC architecture framework (Fig. 14), describing foundational components, the interoperability layer, HSCISs, data services, external systems and digital ecosystems such as regulatory, finance and insurance systems.

blocks.content: Fig 13, 'DIIG digital health enterprise architecture framework'. Within the enterprise, a digital health platform holds shared services (business domain and registry services such as terminology, client, facility, product and health worker registries), data sources (institution-based and population-based) and data services (analytics, dashboards, repositories), joined by an interoperability layer of enabling components. Point-of-service applications below are reused across programmes or used for one use case only; external non-health systems sit to the right; a legend marks investment types. Adapted from the 2020 WHO Digital Implementation Investment Guide.

Fig 14, 'DHSC architecture framework'. Inside a frame labelled DIGITAL HEALTH SUPPLY CHAIN ENTERPRISE: SHARED SERVICES (foundational components: facility, product and supplier registries), DATA SERVICES (analytics — supply chain reports, data warehouse; traceability — track and trace, product verification) and Digital ecosystems (quality, health management information, regulatory, and finance and insurance systems). Below them, an INTEROPERABILITY LAYER of enabling components: authentication, encryption, transformation, orchestration, validation and translation. At the bottom, HEALTH SUPPLY CHAIN INFORMATION SYSTEMS (forecasting and planning, order, warehouse and cold chain management, procurement, supplier and contract management, transportation management and dispensing), beside EXTERNAL SYSTEMS (global platforms, manufacturer systems, data repositories). Callouts explain each layer — for example, that OpenHIM is a useful reference for interoperability components, and SCISMM and TSS v2 for the supply chain systems.

blocks.title: Illustrative architectural approaches and governance options
blocks.content:
Countries often have a mixture of needs and capabilities 
that should be reflected in their DHSC architecture. They 
can adopt an architecture framework using an approach 
that aligns with their supply chain design and level of digital 
maturity. This section provides examples of architectures 
that are based on digital maturity and examples based on 
supply chain design (with different governance options). 
In practice, however, both factors will help determine the 
appropriate architecture framework.
The examples based on digital maturity use the SCISMM 
maturity levels. Levels 1 and 2 invol

summary.text: Chapter 2 section illustrating architectural approaches: maturity-based architectures for moving from SCISMM Level 3 to Level 4 and from Level 4 to Level 5, and supply-chain-design architectures with centralized and decentralized (options A and B) governance (Figs. 15–19), plus the benefits of cross-enterprise analytics services for end-to-end visibility (Fig. 20).

blocks.content: Fig 15, 'Maturity-based architecture: moving from SCISMM Level 3 to Level 4'. The digital health supply chain enterprise has shared services (facility, product and supplier registries) and data services (supply chain reports, data warehouse, track and trace, product verification) above an interoperability layer (authentication, encryption, transformation, orchestration, validation, translation), which connects eight health supply chain information systems: forecasting and planning, order, warehouse and cold chain management, procurement, supplier and contract management, transportation management and dispensing.

Fig 16, 'Maturity-based architecture: moving from SCISMM Level 4 to Level 5'. The level-4 architecture of Fig 15 with analytics and traceability data services, plus a digital ecosystem (quality, health management information, regulatory and finance systems) and external systems (global platforms, manufacturer systems, data repositories) joined through the interoperability layer.

Fig 17, 'Architecture based on supply chain design: centralized management'. Shared and data services, a digital ecosystem and external systems around an interoperability layer that serves a single set of eight health supply chain information systems managed centrally.

Fig 18, 'Architecture based on supply chain design: decentralized management (option A)'. The same services and interoperability layer, with the health supply chain information systems split in two: at national level forecasting and planning, procurement, supplier and contract, transportation, warehouse and cold chain management; at facility level order management, dispensing, inventory and cold chain management.

Fig 19, 'Architecture based on supply chain design: decentralized management (option B)'. The DHSC architecture — shared services, data services, digital ecosystems, an interoperability layer of enabling components, and external systems — with its health supply chain information systems divided by level. At national level: forecasting and planning, procurement, supplier and contract management, transportation management, warehouse management and cold chain management. At district level: procurement, order management, inventory management and cold chain management. At facility level: dispensing.

Fig 20, 'Benefits of cross-enterprise analytics services'. Along the bottom runs the physical supply chain: manufacturing, shipping, regulatory customs, central-warehouse receiving and inventory management, distribution, regional-warehouse replenishment, health-facility dispensing, and patients. Above it sit the planning processes: forecasting and planning; supplier and contract management; procurement; and order management. Dashed arrows carry 'Transactional data from systems relevant to the supply chain' up through the INTEROPERABILITY LAYER into DATA SERVICES — analytics: supply chain reports and a data warehouse. A callout lists the questions analytics services answer: optimizing inventory against consumption to minimize stockouts, whether planned supplies will arrive in time, forecast accuracy against actual consumption, on-time and in-full delivery, wastage and leakage, stock at risk of expiry and where to move it, where and how often stockouts occur, and supplier performance.

blocks.title: Using the DHSC to implement traceability
blocks.content:
Using the DHSC to implement traceability
One key benefit of the DHSC architecture is the ability to track, trace and verify health products. 
Traceability of health products is important to mitigate the risk of falsified medicines and ensure patient 
safety and quality health care. This chapter explores the use of the DHSC architecture framework 
to implement and institutionalize traceability, which requires efforts across multiple areas such as 
regulatory, human resources and processes such as procurement and customs. The chapter focuses 
mainly on deploying technologies that use the DHSC ar

summary.text: Chapter 4 opening on using the DHSC to implement traceability, explaining that the ability to track, trace and verify health products helps mitigate the risk of falsified medicines and ensure patient safety, and that the chapter focuses mainly on deploying technologies that use the DHSC architecture framework to support traceability.

blocks.title: What is traceability?
blocks.content:
The global standards organization GS1 describes traceability 
as the ability “to see the movement of health products across 
the supply chain” (25). Traceability means being able to trace 
the path of health care products from the manufacturer 
to individuals, identifying ownership changes at different 
points along the supply chain. Traceability also aids in the 
whereabouts of products at any given moment, including 
their intended route towards the point of dispensing.

summary.text: Chapter 4 section defining traceability, citing GS1's description as the ability to see the movement of health products across the supply chain, and explaining it as tracing the path of products from manufacturer to individuals, identifying ownership changes and showing products' whereabouts.

blocks.title: Why is traceability important?
blocks.content:
Tracing and tracking enhance the efficiency and integrity 
of the health supply chain. By providing global visibility 
into every change of product ownership along the supply 
chain, traceability helps identify falsified health products 
and prevents their dispensation to individuals (among other 
benefits, which include efficiencies in inventory management 
and prevention of medicine shortages), ultimately helping to 
ensure patient safety. Traceability thus plays an important 
role in ensuring quality health care for individuals.
Traceability also supports the ability to manage product 
reca

summary.text: Chapter 4 section on why traceability is important, explaining how visibility of ownership changes helps identify falsified products, protect patient safety and manage product recalls, and noting that traceability systems are mostly based on regulatory requirements, require global harmonization and rely on global standards for interoperability.

blocks.title: Traceability models
blocks.content:
The three main models for implementing traceability are the 
centralized, semi-centralized and distributed models. They 
differ mostly in how they store the data and share them with 
the relevant health authority and across actors in the supply 
chain. The centralized model involves a single database 
or repository for storing all traceability data. In a semi-
centralized model, the traceability data are spread across 
multiple databases or repositories. In the distributed model, 
traceability data are maintained separately by each supply 
chain partner. 
This handbook does not recommend a par

summary.text: Chapter 4 section on traceability models, describing centralized, semi-centralized and distributed models, the essential technology components for a centralized model (foundational components, repository, interoperability layer, HSCISs and traceability analytics), track and trace through DHSC components (Fig. 24), factors such as master data quality and manufacturer marking, and an illustrative traceability service interface (Fig. 25).

blocks.content: Fig 24, 'Achieving track and trace capabilities through DHSC architecture components'. Along the bottom, the supply chain runs from regulator through central, regional and district warehouses to health facilities and patients. Each location's system — regulator systems, warehouse management, transportation management, inventory management, dispensing, and verification at the patient — exchanges data in both directions with the INTEROPERABILITY LAYER, as do the external systems (global platforms, manufacturer systems, data repositories). Above the layer, DATA SERVICES hold analytics and traceability (track and trace, product verification). A callout lists the questions traceability services answer: where a batch is now, whether supply chain integrity was maintained, who had custody on a date, where a batch was dispensed, whether the product moved through known locations, whether there were anomalies, and whether the product is genuine. A legend defines traceability data as what (product, batch and serial number), when, where and why (the transaction type).

Fig 25, 'Illustrative example of a traceability service interface'. At the top is a mock screen, 'Track and trace results for product 001001123123', batch A1001234. It shows a timeline of five verified events with their location and timestamp: verified and received at the central warehouse (11 Mar 2023); shipped from the central warehouse (5 Apr); verified and received at health facility 001 (6 Apr); verified and dispensed there (10 Apr); and a final patient-side verification of serial number 202 with GPS coordinates (10 Apr, 16:14). Below, the flow that produces it: the manufacturer, central/regional warehouse and health facilities emit ship, receive and dispense events, and handheld verify scans are made along the way. All of these feed DATA SERVICES (analytics and traceability), which answer the screen's query for the product code, batch, its serial numbers 201 to 204 and the expiry date.

blocks.content: Figs 26 and 27, current-state (March 2024) and future-state supply chain systems in Ethiopia. Current state: an OpenHIM interoperability layer, a master health facility registry, a national product catalogue under development and terminology services, DHIS2 and EMR, and supply chain systems including VITAS, FANOS, DAGU, eLMIS, eAPTs and eRIS, with eTrade and eCustom as external systems; a legend colours each by its state. summary.text: Chapter 5 country example of Malawi's DHSC initiative, describing the Supply Chain Systems Architecture (SCSA) developed in 2021 under the HTSS division of the MOH with USAID GHSC-PSM support and approved in September 2022, current overlapping HSCISs as of December 2023 (Fig. 28), the future-state architecture using the National Product Catalog (Figs. 29–30), insights and the supply chain structure.

blocks.content: Figs 28 and 29, current-state (December 2023) and future-state supply chain systems in Malawi. Current state: OpenHIM, a master health facility registry, national product catalogue and terminology services, DHIS2, QAT and QuanTB for forecasting, OpenLMIS for orders, Navision for warehouse and procurement, eHIN for dispensing, cStock for inventory, GFPVAN outside. Future state: a supplier registry, supply chain reports, a data warehouse, track and trace and product verification are added; E-GP for procurement and contracts, a new transportation system, OpenLMIS and cStock at facility level, and parallel supply chains among external systems.

Fig 30, 'Visualization of future-state architecture from Malawi's SCSA'. Layers from top: analytics and business intelligence (data warehouse, dashboards, reports, traceability, returns and recalls, verification); an OpenHIM interoperability layer; national supply chain information systems (procurement, forecasting and planning, supplier and contract, warehouse and transportation management) beside facility systems (OpenLMIS, cStock, eHIN); a second interoperability layer; and regulatory and foundational components (product item registration, product registry, facility registry, supplier registry, terminology). A global GFPVAN and manufacturers link from the left. Adapted from Malawi's 2022 Supply Chain Systems Architecture.
